paragrafos: Chagas disease is caused by a parasite carried by an insect that lives in the walls of poor housing. Around 8 million people are infected, more than 100 million are at risk, and about 30,000 new cases appear every year across 21 endemic countries in the Americas. It kills more than 10,000 people annually — most of them decades after infection, when the parasite has quietly damaged the heart.

Two drugs exist, benznidazole and nifurtimox. Both date from the 1960s and 70s. They work reasonably well in the acute phase, poorly in the chronic phase where most patients are, and roughly 3% of people treated develop severe adverse reactions. No better drug has replaced them in fifty years.
Not because the science is impossible. Because the people who get this disease cannot pay for the research. That is what makes it a target worth computing on.

fontes.texto: PAHO — Chagas disease in the Americas

paragrafos: CYP51 is the enzyme the parasite uses to build the sterols in its own membrane. Block it and the parasite cannot maintain its cell wall. It is the same family of enzyme that antifungal drugs target, which is why it is one of the best-characterised targets in the field.

It was chosen over cruzain — the target this project screened first and rejected — for a structural reason measured here: cruzain has a shallow, open cleft where the scoring function could not tell the true crystal pose from a wrong one. CYP51 has a deep, enclosed pocket with a haem at the bottom, which forces a binding geometry that docking can read.

Stated plainly: posaconazole, a CYP51 inhibitor, was tested in humans for chronic Chagas disease and failed as a single therapy. That is a real mark against this target and we are not hiding it. It does not invalidate the screen — the failure was of that molecule's efficacy, not of the enzyme's role — but anyone evaluating this project should know it.

chembl_humano_nota: Human CYP51, for selectivity: a compound that blocks the parasite enzyme and the human one is not a candidate.
